title: The chariot of fire (2 Kings 2)
hook: Elisha asks a double portion of Elijah's spirit, and the mantle falls

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elijah at Horeb, and God in a whisper. Your line was a whistling of a gentle air.

Elijah is walking his last road, and everyone seems to know it, Elijah too. His young disciple Elisha, Eliseus in the Douay-Rheims, walks beside him. At each town, Elijah says: stay here, the Lord has sent me on ahead. And three times Elisha answers: "As the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee." At Bethel and again at Jericho, the sons of the prophets come out and ask Elisha: you know the Lord is taking your master today? And he says: I know. Hold your peace. They reach the Jordan.
screen: `ELIJAH'S LAST ROAD.` → `I WILL NOT LEAVE THEE.` → `I KNOW. HOLD YOUR PEACE.`

segments.voice: At the river, Elijah rolls up his mantle, the rough cloak that marked him as a prophet, and strikes the water. It parts, and the two cross on dry ground, the way Israel once crossed. Then Elijah asks: what shall I do for thee, before I be taken away? And Elisha asks big. The Douay says "thy double spirit"; many English Bibles say a double portion. In Israel, a firstborn son inherited a double share. Elisha is asking to be Elijah's heir, his son in the spirit. Elijah says: thou hast asked a hard thing. If you see me when I'm taken, it's yours. They keep walking and talking. Suddenly a chariot of fire with horses of fire comes between them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. The chariot separates them; the whirlwind carries him up. Elisha sees it and cries out: "My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the driver thereof." He tears his clothes in grief. Then he looks down. Elijah's mantle has fallen. He picks it up, walks back to the Jordan, and strikes the water with it, asking, where is the God of Elijah? The water parts. The prophets watching from across the river say: the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha. It's a scene about handing on. A teacher doesn't live forever, but what God gave through him can pass to another, the way a cloak falls into new hands. And Elijah's story isn't finished: centuries later he appears with Moses beside Jesus on the mountain of the Transfiguration.
screen: `THE MANTLE PARTS THE JORDAN.` · `ASKING FOR A DOUBLE PORTION.` · `CHARIOT BETWEEN, WHIRLWIND UP.` · `THE MANTLE FALLS TO ELISHA.` · then, large: `MY FATHER, MY FATHER, THE CHARIOT OF ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something that lasted, a grandparent who showed you how to pray, a coach, a priest or sister, a friend through a hard year, maybe someone gone now. Picture what they left you, a habit, a phrase, a way of treating people, and pick up that mantle. If you pray, ask that some of what was in them carry on in you.
Elisha. The disciple who watched Elijah taken up by a whirlwind, and picked up the mantle that fell to him. Today's word.
Your line: pick up the mantle. The cloak falls, and the spirit rests on another. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Elijah's taking up and Elisha's call in the weekday Mass readings, and remember both on their feast days in the Carmelite calendar; Elijah appears again in the Gospel of the Transfiguration, read each Lent and on August 6.

original.note: Hebrew: mantle, a cloak. Elijah's adderet marked him as a prophet, and fell to Elisha.

what a scholar hears: the double portion is the firstborn's inheritance in Deuteronomy 21:17; Elisha asks to be Elijah's heir, and is then seen doing what Elijah did.

chat.meaning: Elijah's mantle fell to Elisha, who struck the Jordan with it; the prophets saw that Elijah's spirit rested on him.

notes: The Carmelite calendar keeps Elijah (July 20) and Elisha (June 14); confirm the dates and that howItsDone is accurate.
The Transfiguration Gospel is read on the Second Sunday of Lent and the feast of August 6; confirm.
Double portion as the firstborn's share (Deuteronomy 21:17): standard reading; confirm.
Reviewer corrected the hook: the sons of the prophets meet Elisha at Bethel and Jericho (2:3, 2:5), not at every town; 'hold your peace' follows the Douay.
'The way Israel once crossed' alludes to the Red Sea and Joshua's crossing of the Jordan; confirm.
